newsitem.title: USA: Chinese diplomats, scholars shun U.S. conference.
newsitem.headline: Chinese diplomats, scholars shun U.S. conference.

text.p: Several Chinese diplomats and scholars have withdrawn from a U.S. conference on China apparently because a Chinese pro-democracy leader was also invited to speak, organizers said on Friday.

They were among a wide range of China experts invited by the World Affairs Council of Northern California to its annual conference this weekend in Pacific Grove, California. The theme of the conference is "China: The Next Superpower?"

The council, a non-profit group that discusses foreign affairs, issued a statement expressing surprise at the "sudden withdrawal" of three Chinese diplomats and scholars who had been due to speak at the conference.
Council president David Fischer said he was disappointed by the decision which he said could "only undercut the dialogue we seek between the U.S. and China."

Fischer said he believed the decision to "boycott" the conference was connected to the invitation of Li Lu, a leader of the pro-democracy movement who fled China after the 1989 Tiananmen Square crackdown.
Li's name had not been in early versions of the program when the Chinese officials had agreed to attend.

Among those who withdrew were Zhang Wenpu and Sun Aqing, members of the Chinese People's Institute of Foreign Affairs, a quasi-official thinktank that the World Affairs Council said was closely connected to China's top leadership.
Professor Zhiyong Xiong, dean of academic studies at the Foreign Affairs College, Beijing, also canceled.

Zhang, a former Chinese ambassador to Canada, had agreed to give the keynote address but pulled out, citing health problems, the council said. The other two guests, who had also previously accepted invitations, canceled verbally following Zhang's withdrawal, it said.
A fourth Chinese representative -- Song Zengshou, China's consul general in San Francisco -- wrote Fischer this week declining an invitation to attend the conference because he was otherwise engaged.

In the letter, he said he thought it was inappropriate to invite Li to the conference because he "is a criminal who has violated China's laws. His anti-China position and speech, I'm sure, will have negative impact on the conference as well as on the development of Sino-U.S. relations."
"It'll be appreciated if you take proper action to stop his attendance," the consul general wrote.

World Affairs Council officials said they would not cancel Li's invitation. "We knew we were taking a risk in extending invitations to a broad spectrum of opinion, but we simply cannot let anyone determine who we will invite to speak in California," Fischer said.
U.S. Rep. Nancy Pelosi, a Democrat who is often critical of China, is also scheduled to speak at the conference, which is expected to draw about 750 people.
A spokesman at China's Consulate General in San Francisco could not immediately be reached for comment.
